display_name: List held authorizations — what is blocked on or owed by a role right now
description: Held-authorization queue (R1 2026-08-17; accepted obligations added for wgr_d854aa6c). Read-only answer to "what is blocked on <role>?" for a session with zero memory of a prior seat — a freshly-booted or freshly-rotated Git-Controller or coordinator, an operator checking status, or any peer wondering why a request has gone quiet. Returns two kinds of entry, each marked by entry_kind: refusal entries (requests Git-Controller refused, logged with record_held_authorization) and accepted entries (authorizations a seat accepted whose act has not fired, logged with record_accepted_authorization). Acceptance is never inferred from a refusal's reason text. By default it returns open refusals (retired_at unset) and pending accepted entries (state accepted); include_retired adds retired refusals and fired, withdrawn or retired accepted entries. Optional owed_by_role / requesting_peer filters compose with AND across both kinds. Entries come one page at a time, refusals first and then accepted entries, oldest first: limit sets the page size (1-100, default 100) and next_cursor continues it. A reader may conclude nothing is outstanding only after paging until next_cursor is null. An accepted entry shows its current act, predicate and authorizing_message_id; get_authorization_history shows the predicates it withdrew. Never filters or flags by age itself — this queue has no silent TTL by design (a queue that silently forgets is worse than no queue), so created_at is returned as-is and the caller judges staleness directly. Every entry is an obligation, never proof that an authorization is valid and never landing permission.
embedding_description: Checking what is blocked on or owed by a role after a rotation: requests Git-Controller refused, plus authorizations a seat accepted that have not fired yet and still wait on a precondition. The read a fresh successor runs instead of scrolling a transcript, showing who owes what, each current predicate, and when it was recorded.

result_processor_customizations.result_description: {"entries": [{entry_kind ('refusal'|'accepted'), entry_id, requesting_peer, owed_by_role, branch_or_request_ref, reason, created_at, retired_at, retired_reason, retired_by, state, version, authorizing_message_id, act, predicate, notes, terminal_reason, terminal_actor, terminal_evidence}, ...], "count": N, "next_cursor": "..."|null}. A refusal entry carries reason and the retired_* stamps with the accepted fields null; an accepted entry carries the accepted fields with reason and retired_* null.
result_processor_customizations.presentation_guidance: An empty list with next_cursor null is good news (nothing blocked or owed) and should read as such. A non-empty list — especially one with an old created_at — is worth calling out plainly: name who is blocked or which act is owed, by whom, and on which current predicate. Never present an accepted entry as permission to land; it is an obligation to check against its predicate.

error_processor_customizations.action_context: A paged state read of held_authorization (refusals) and accepted_authorization (accepted obligations), filtered by the optional owed_by_role / requesting_peer, and by retired_at IS NULL and state accepted unless include_retired is set, oldest first.
error_processor_customizations.error_interpretation: invalid_argument: limit is not an integer from 1 through 100. invalid_cursor: cursor is not a next_cursor this verb returned. state_service_unavailable: the state service is not bound.
error_processor_customizations.recovery_guidance: invalid_argument or invalid_cursor means fix the call; restart from the first page without a cursor. state_service_unavailable is worth a retry once the platform is up. This verb issues no writes and is always safe to retry.
